#9957. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9956. The anti-marketing aspect of the Gemini network

I like Gemini. Not the Google Chatbot but the network that existed before Google named its product. If you are enough of a geek, you may want to give it a try.

Eoin is counting the number of "capsules" on the Gemini network. A capsule is the equivalent of a "website" on the Web or a "hole" on Gopher. It’s a personal space, a bunch of pages. Blogs become "gemlogs".

Eoin’s first observation is that the number of active capsules is slowly growing. The network is healthy.

But his second observation is really interesting: there’s absolutely no correlation between the number of new capsules in a given month and articles about the Gemini protocol being promoted on the first page of Hacker News.

This is a confirmation of what I’ve been trying to explain for years: your metrics and web statistics are completely useless. The number of visitors, the number of clicks are worthless if you are not a marketer trying to extract money from a big brand. They don’t mean anything.

By the way: you should really avoid Hacker News these days. The front page is heavily manipulated to promote pro-AI stuff and bury everything that might question wether fascism-capitalism is good.

A Mozilla employee is leaving after 15 years and comes to a similar conclusion. Mozilla is awesome because it has always been abnormal. It is mostly used by abnormal people. This means that hiring "normal managers" who try to make it "normal" and chase "normal" metrics is, of course, a recipe for failure.

I always failed to understand those marketing people who try to be "like others but a bit cheaper". While all the value is being different enough to nurture your own niche.

I completely removed statistics from my blog in 2013. At the time, I had a very strong realisation that the blog posts that mattered most, those I was proudest of, and those that prompted people to mail me even years later all had mediocre statistics.

On the contrary, most of my hit, my "buzz", were quickly forgotten. But, being addicted to statistics, I was unconsciously adapting my writing style to improve those numbers. I was scrolling through social media posts that were highly popular while trying to create some myself.

Closing my social media accounts and, instead, procrastinating on Gemini had the opposite effect: making me read other ideas without caring about reactions, about popularity. Jsreed5 made the same observation while he was trying the Nostr protocol. While Nostr’s technicalities may be interesting by themselves, the content on it is similar to the one found of mainstream social networks. And our smolnet Gemini-formatted brains cannot take it anymore!

We really need a simple Gemini hosting provider that would also provide a Web version, to welcome less technical-minded people who still may want to access a quieter, non-commercial, out-of-time virtual space.

Lot of people are trying Gemini and find that there’s no content on it, that they can’t have their news and dopamine hit on it. Well, that’s exactly the point.

The fact that only a niche minority want to use it is also part of the point. Gemini might not be for you. That’s fine. The modern Web and even the real world (where every device is actively working against me and every human interaction seems to be about AI) is increasingly not for me. So let me have my strange niche space.

UPDATE: Those Gemini hosting providers exist:

I write science-fiction novels in French. For Bikepunk, my new post-apocalyptic-cyclist book, my publisher is looking for contacts in other countries to distribute it in languages other than French. If you can help, contact me!

#9955. Glasswing overwhelms maintainers with underwhelming findings (VulnCheck)

Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has written a blog post that looks at vulnerabilities found by Anthropic's Project Glasswing since it launched on April 7, and finds it wanting:

Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as "True Positives".

[...] AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

So I'm not super surprised if not many of 40,000 potential security bugs have actually made it to "really fixed" yet.

Unusual/stale? Posted Nov 12, 2026 22:17 UTC (Thu) by Vorpal (guest, #136011) [Link] This very much matches my experience at my dayjob as well. For patch code review LLMs can be really good, with some false positives (but quite few). They find things (most) humans would never think about, especially about interactions with entirely different parts of the code base. That said, they also miss things humans wouldn't, for example about overall system design. And, as you said, the author generally have the code fresh in their mind making it easy to deal with the feedback. We have also tried finding security issues with LLMs and there it was much more of a mixed bag. A few were genuine bugs, but many of those weren't actually security issues or even worth fixing (e.g. "yes this is a theoretical bug in things we are sending, if you assume another part of the same application building on top of this staticly linked library is actively malicious, and since this is C++, almost everything assumes the API user isn't 'holding it wrong'."). And a fair share were straight up incorrect. And of course, typically no one knows exactly what the code does off the top of their heads (some parts of the code even date to the late 90s), so triaging takes way more time than dealing with feedback on a PR. It is interesting to me that LLMs does so much poorly in one area than another.

Before AI, people were trusting random stuff online way too much. You can be unlucky and meet bad people in real life but the chances are reasonably low because most people are decent. But before AI there were still a few practical limits, even online. So people were still falling for it. Now thanks to AI, those practical limits are gone. Good riddance. Some of the current AI backslash might also be caused to that. I mean not just caused by energy, water, inflation and layoffs but also by the increase of online garbage. This is a good instance of "It must get worse before it gets better". Or some sort of "tradegy of the commons" for bad guys? Who knows, this might even get people to spend less time online?

I wasn't including "online media", I was only referring to _unknown and unsolicited_ media. Whether you are consuming Fox News or the New York Times, it's really not hard to verify that you are really consuming those and not some impersonation. That particular problem is basically solved. Once you have verified that what you see actually came from Fox News or the New York Times and you know who's talking (first, critical _identification_ step), then should you _trust_ them? (second step) Trusting _identified_ sources is a very different question that I wasn't touching on. Because the answer is the same that it's always has been: 1. Find who pays them (often: not you!) 2. Count the number of mistakes, lies and contradictions over long periods of time. 3. Shortcut: ask people you trust who have been doing that work. That is how trust always gets built: with transitive reputation and over time. There is nothing new in those second step, trust processes, the global village and AI did not change anything and do not matter here. If people starting trusting _random_ stuff less and less thanks to AI garbage as I'm hoping in the previous comment, then the "traditional", pre-Internet trust systems will hopefully start working better again. Cause the former has been leveraging our confirmation bias and other bad instincts to actively harm the latter. With long and deep enough observation you can gauge not just the reliability when reporting facts but also the bias when expressing opinions. Assuming there is a clear distinction between the two in the first place - if not then run. You must constantly monitor the reliability of your shortcuts/friends/gurus too. Confirmation bias is an even higher risk there. Good education teaches that too. > how can you verify anything anymore ? You can't always verify everything yourself. That's why trust (and of course: free speech) exist. One thing I like to do is to read articles that teach me nothing on a topic I'm already very familiar with: great way to assert reliability. For instance: computer stuff in mainstream media.

InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read

Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our new learning.

Debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:

Every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao said. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

Technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we update our understanding, Yao explained:

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

#9953. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9952. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Show interactive benchmark results with downloadable data

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

#9951. Rust 1.100.0 released

Version 1.100.0 of the Rust language has been released. Notable changes include the stabilization of the never type, core parts of the Allocator API, reporting of unused dependencies in Cargo, and more.

Talking about unused deps and dead code removal: I'm still a C developer, and the C language has many tools, but I don't know a tool that works for shared libraries (with unstable API) with code scattered in multiple repositories (for a monorepo that's easier). Do you know the existence of such tool? C is a more "greppable" language than Rust, so I simply use `git grep` for each symbol, but it can be time consuming. Rust and other modern languages facilitate a lot this task. (Sorry if it's slightly off-topic for a Rust news).

But it's not that big a deal because it's the dependencies in Cargo, the tool that will fetch external dependencies, not the C equivalent of #include for which there was already a warning. Also, like said in the release notes, it should check all the build target, so the C equivalent of checking all the #ifdef, so you can't just compile one time and check if the symbols are used.

From a security point of view, was fetching an unused dependency a potential attack vector? (like changing global state even without calling exported functions or using global data). A little like the use of pkg-config in C. pkg-config is usable (mainly) thanks to packaging efforts done by distributions, so it's not an upstream-only thing (unlike Cargo, Npm, PyPI, etc).

#9950. Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Europe's supermarket freezer hacks show how security issues can cascade across an industry, disrupting supply chains at scale.

The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center (C4) on Nov. 9 published a five page report attributing the series of attacks on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and specifically on the IRGC's Shahid Shoostari and Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive units.

France's Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country will propose to its European partners new sanctions against the Iranian entities and individuals allegedly involved in the cyberattack, adding that France reserves the right to take additional proportionate measures to respond to the attacks.

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

This story was updated at 2:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 9 to reflect France's accusations against Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

#9949. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#9948. AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Security records are increasingly being used by vendors to train their models, creating new risks for enterprises.

Traditionally, security incident records have served a singular, very important purpose: to document what the organization observed, decided, and did. Closure notes, rule text, false-positive dispositions, and the reason why an alert was dropped are treated by security teams as records contained in the ticket queue. For organizations to reconstruct their decisions and, crucially, be accountable for them later, all of this evidence must be retained.

To be sure, security automation is anything but new. For years, SOAR platforms have executed playbooks, closed alerts, and recorded dispositions. They run a rule that customers wrote. The change is what happens to the record afterward, as a portion of the evidence has an alternate destination for a different purpose. Once incident records are ingested into a security AI system with permission to capture data for model building or validation, this evidence can become data the vendor uses for model development and validation.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

A sufficiently large collection of prompts and related records can offer more than a glimpse into which signals are treated by the organization as meaningful, which detections are suppressed, what analysts mark as benign, and where it misses something.

A single closure is a comparatively harmless note. A series, however, presents a map; suppressing the same class of alerts delineates boundaries of concern. The rationales for closures indicate acceptable levels of PowerShell noise or failed logins that warrant a ticket. Tuning decisions encode which signals the team stops trusting and when. The contents of the ticket do not need to be accessed by an external party for it to understand the pattern, which is the sensitive portion.

This isn't about reconstructing an AI incident; that's a logging decision. Nor is it about prompt injection, or the familiar case of a vendor training on customer chat logs. The problem is what happens when ordinary security records acquire a second use.

Microsoft Security Copilot provides an option for the owner to allow Microsoft to capture and human-review Security Copilot data to enhance and validate Microsoft's security-specific model, which is built on the Azure OpenAI foundation model. The data captured for model improvement can include whatever Microsoft plug-ins and Security Copilot agents have used while interacting with the product. The documentation states that this data is not used to train the foundation model and is not shared with OpenAI. A second setting controls the capture of data for the purpose of product-performance reviews.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

The default for each setting depends on the method of provisioning the workspace. With the exception of Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 auto-provisioning, data sharing is enabled by default. The customer that enabled the setting has made an intentional decision, but the customer that has not viewed the settings page may not know which default applies. Using the service and allowing a vendor to capture data for model development or validation are different decisions, and Microsoft has already made them separable.

The archive had one job: namely, to help the organization reconstruct and defend its own decisions. Now the same records may be held by a vendor for model development or validation, which in turn creates new risks. A vendor breach puts the records outside the customer's network, while a legal demand can expose them without the customer's control. The retention rules and access controls were built for an archive the organization controlled, but they were not built for a second copy elsewhere.

An auditable record has to preserve more than the final decision. It has to distinguish what the organization knew, what the analyst decided, what the system was given, and what the system recommended. Otherwise, the model's observation effectively becomes the decision. Counsel asking what the organization knew at the time of the incident will not be satisfied by this. An auditor asking why the detections were tuned down should not be met with the closure rationale that also appears in the evidence stream.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

This belongs in the procurement contract. A vendor's use of customer security records to provide a service does not by itself authorize their use for model improvement, and evidence retention and model development are different things that should require separate permission. Rule content, closure notes, and ticket text should not be covered by a generic AI clause. If the vendor wants the data for model improvement, then this should be an explicit, revocable choice.

Until these uses are formally separated, the archive has two functions. One of them continues, as expected, to be operated by the organization. The other turns all the evidence into the vendor's resource.

#9946. UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The UK is betting on domestic AI and cyber investment to reduce reliance on US tech — but security leaders question whether the funding is too fragmented and too late.

The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access to the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of the UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that became embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customers a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"
