#9932. Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Attackers can exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that Anthropic's AI assistant can access and run on a user's machine.

An attacker can use a flaw in Anthropic Claude's document-processing tool to run malicious code on Linux systems just by creating a temporary file that the AI assistant can access. The flaw highlights a growing risk posed by even trusted AI tools to introduce security gaps in enterprise environments.

Researchers from AIR Security discovered the flaw, which they've dubbed "Office Party," in Anthropic's official DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX skills, which are tools that enable Claude to create, read, edit, and process Microsoft Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets, respectively.

The vulnerability stems from a helper script, soffice.py, that launches LibreOffice to convert documents, including rendering Word documents as PDFs, they revealed in a report published today. When the script encounters an environment where Unix-domain sockets cannot be opened, it uses a workaround that loads a shared library through the Linux LD_PRELOAD mechanism.

Related:N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

Anthropic has opted not to fix the issue.

During conversation, the script checks whether a library named lo_socket_shim.so already exists in a shared temporary directory but does not verify its origin or contents. An attacker who can place a malicious library at that location before the next document-processing operation can potentially have their code loaded and executed within LibreOffice, with the privileges of the user running the AI agent.

In this way, the flaw can allow attackers to execute malicious code on a user's Linux machine by exploiting an unverified file path used during document conversion, explains Niv Hoffman, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of AIR Research Lab, in an email interview.

"An attacker gets one malicious file into a shared temporary folder which many programs use, and the next time an employee asks Claude for a document, Anthropic's trusted skill loads that file and runs it," he tells Dark Reading.

The vulnerability affects Linux environments where Unix sockets are blocked, including certain container security configurations, and Claude Code's sandbox. AIR Security reports that macOS is not affected because it does not load the library through LD_PRELOAD.

The AIR researchers demonstrated two ways the attack can work on Linux systems. In one scenario, they manually placed a malicious library in the temporary directory before asking Claude Code to generate a document. In another, they used a separate, seemingly legitimate AI skill to unpack a supporting file into the same directory. When the document-processing skill subsequently ran, the malicious library was loaded automatically.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The flaw presents a serious issue for enterprises running Linux because it exploits "the default skills that all Claude agents use — [of which there are] hundreds of millions — and one planted file can make them run an attacker’s code with the employee's own access," Hoffman explains.

This second attack scenario is particularly concerning for enterprise security teams because it illustrates how individually benign-looking AI skills can interact to create an attack chain. And often, "companies don't have visibility to which skills and other agent add-ons they have installed, and don't have a red button to revoke or patch a vulnerable one," Hoffman explains.

Moreover, a malicious or compromised skill does not necessarily need to exploit the document-processing tool directly; it may simply need to place a file that another trusted component will execute, according to the AIR researchers.

The AIR team discovered the flaw in May and reported it to Anthropic, which acknowledged its existence, according to the report. However, the AI company "considers it outside its security boundary, since the vulnerable code only runs inside a sandbox," AIR Research Lab's Omri Saxena and Or Nevo wrote in the report. This means that as of now, the helper script still uses the same fixed path and still loads whatever file it finds there, they said.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Hoffman says that Anthropic's response is "not quite" adequate, "because even if the skills run within a sandbox, the attacker’s code then runs inside it with the user's own permissions, where the user's files and work already are," he says. Anthropic did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment about whether the company would take any further action to remedy the issue.

For businesses deploying AI agents and coding assistants, Office Party reinforces the need to treat AI skills as software dependencies rather than trusted extensions, and secure them as such, according to AIR.

To mitigate, organizations should make it a point to know "exactly what skills or add-ons an organization is using with Claude Code by keeping a live inventory of every AI skill and add-on across employees' agents," Hoffman says. They also should "review even official ones like any other code, and update or patch the whole set whenever a new vulnerability is published."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9930. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#9928. Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Inaugural edition by Informa Markets in India brings together leading researchers, security practitioners and industry decision makers for four days of cutting-edge research, technical exchange and strategic dialogue.

13 Trainings delivered by 19 trainers, 70+ Summit speakers, 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers, and 2,000+ Business Hall delegates across four days.

Black Hat Arsenal featured 44 open-source security tool demonstrations across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs.

Keynotes by leading cybersecurity experts Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), and Nathan Hamiel (Kudelski Security), alongside a special address by Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

Key themes included AI security, digital payment fraud, emerging cyber threats and post-quantum readiness.

Bengaluru, November 5, 2026 — Black Hat India 2026, organised by Informa Markets in India, concluded its inaugural edition at the Sheraton Grand, Brigade Gateway, Bengaluru, following four days of high-impact training, leadership discussions, original technical research and industry engagement from October 27 to 30, 2026.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is one of the world's most respected cybersecurity conference series, renowned for its independent, vendor-neutral research and technical depth. Its debut in India marks a significant milestone for the country's cybersecurity ecosystem, bringing a globally recognised platform and its international community of researchers and practitioners to one of the world's fastest-growing digital economies.

The inaugural edition brought together a diverse mix of technical training, strategic discussions, cutting-edge research and hands-on engagement, with each day offering a distinct experience for the cybersecurity community.

Day 1 opened with specialised Trainings, featuring 13 hands-on courses delivered by 19 trainers and covering subjects ranging from offensive security fundamentals to securing emerging AI systems.

Day 2 was dedicated to Summit Day, bringing together 70+ speakers and 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers across two tracks, Frontier AI Security and CISO Strategy. Discussions examined the changing cybersecurity landscape, enterprise risk and the growing strategic responsibilities of security leaders.

Days 3 and 4 featured the Briefings and Business Hall, with 35 researchers and practitioners presenting original work on emerging threats, software and cloud security, AI and digital identity, while welcoming more than 2,000 Business Hall delegates. A major attraction was Black Hat Arsenal, where 44 presenters demonstrated open-source security tools across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs, enabling attendees to engage directly with developers and explore practical security applications.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The event brought together prominent government representatives, industry leaders and international cybersecurity experts. Summit Day was inaugurated in the presence of Lt. Gen. Rajesh Pant and Lt. Gen. M.U. Nair, both former National Cyber Security Coordinators of India; Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA); and Brijesh Singh, IPS, Principal Secretary, Government of Maharashtra.

Dr. Bahl's keynote examined the implications of emerging AI technologies for India's digital ecosystem and the importance of strengthening cyber resilience. Nathan Hamiel, Senior Director of Research at Kudelski Security, delivered the Briefings keynote, exploring how AI is transforming cybersecurity and why human expertise remains indispensable. Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, delivered a special address on transnational cybercrime.

Related:Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Senior representatives from NPCI, the Reserve Bank of India, NCIIPC, PhonePe, CRED, Razorpay, Groww, Reliance, Adani Enterprises, HCLTech, EY, Deloitte, KPMG, Microsoft, Mandiant, Akamai, Zscaler and Zoho participated alongside independent and academic researchers.

Across the programme, discussions consistently highlighted the growing importance of securing and governing AI, the increasing sophistication of cyberattacks, software supply-chain vulnerabilities, digital payment fraud and deepfakes. Protecting India's Digital Public Infrastructure, preparing for post-quantum technologies and translating technical risks into business priorities also emerged as important themes.

India's rapid digital expansion is creating unprecedented opportunities, alongside an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. The average organisational cost of a data breach in India reached ₹25.5 crore in 2026, nearly 16% higher year on year, underlining the growing economic implications of cyber risk.

Commenting on the significance of Black Hat India's successful maiden edition, Mr. Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director, Informa Markets in India, said, "India’s rapid digital transformation has unlocked extraordinary opportunities, while also bringing the need to secure an increasingly connected economy into sharper focus. In the last financial year, UPI processed over 24,000 crore transactions worth more than ₹314 lakh crore, while CERT-In reported over 29.4 lakh cybersecurity incidents in 2025, an increase of approximately 44% over the previous year. The recent spate of global cyber incidents, including critical PHP vulnerabilities, being described as ‘Black October’, is a timely reminder that digital growth must be matched by stronger security and resilience.

The successful debut of Black Hat India is a significant achievement for us and an important addition to India’s cybersecurity ecosystem. The scale of participation and quality of discussions reflect the strong appetite for a platform of this calibre. As AI reshapes the threat landscape, staying ahead of emerging risks becomes even more critical. We are proud to have brought this globally recognised platform to India and look forward to building on this strong beginning,” he added.

The inaugural edition was supported by Diamond Partners TrendAI, Upwind and EY, alongside other sponsors and exhibitors, and shaped by the Black Hat India Review Board.

Black Hat India's debut comes in a milestone year for Informa Markets in India, marking 20 years of its presence in the country. The edition is also part of Festivity of Business, the company's annual campaign, now in its seventh year. Spanning 100 days, the campaign celebrates the optimism, energy and entrepreneurial spirit driving India's growth, bringing together the country's vibrant festive season and its high season of business events.

The successful inaugural edition establishes a significant new platform for India's cybersecurity community, bringing global expertise, original research and industry leadership together at a time when securing the digital future has never been more important.

For more information, visit www.blackhat-india.com.

Black Hat India extends the globally recognised Black Hat platform to India's rapidly evolving cybersecurity landscape in Bengaluru, connecting the country's growing community of information security professionals with global research, expertise and industry developments. The platform brings together cybersecurity practitioners, researchers, technology leaders and organisations to exchange knowledge, examine emerging security challenges and explore advancements in information security. Through its technical Briefings, specialised Trainings and industry engagement, Black Hat India provides opportunities for professional development, collaboration and knowledge sharing, while strengthening connections between India's cybersecurity ecosystem and the global security community.

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is an internationally recognized cybersecurity event series providing the most technical and relevant information security research. Grown from a single annual conference to the most respected information security event series internationally, these multi-day events provide the security community with the latest cutting-edge research, developments, and trends. Black Hat Briefings and Trainings are driven by the needs of the global security community, striving to bring together the best minds in the industry. Black Hat inspires professionals at all career levels, encouraging growth and collaboration among academia, world-class researchers and leaders in the public and private sectors. Today, Black Hat Briefings and Trainings are held annually in the United States, Europe, and Asia, providing premier venues for elite security researchers and trainers to find their audience.

Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. Agentic AI architecture extends microservices and cloud-native architectures with AI agents that work with context, memory, and protocols such as MCP and A2A. The article covers bounded-context integration, task-dependent coordination strategies, new security risks, and observability needs. It expects gradual adoption alongside existing architectures, with platforms absorbing common components.

Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations The Influence Toolkit

Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

Henry Wilson is Senior Architect in the BBC’s Product Group, responsible for backend audio teams. Having worked as a Principal Engineer and Senior Architect at the BBC, he focuses on technical leadership, organizational influence, and senior IC career pathways while guiding complex backend systems and engineering teams.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Henry Wilson: I want to start today with a thought exercise. I want you to think about what single skill makes you excel in your current job. I'm sure some of you are thinking about your technical skills, your ability to design architectures, to write code or to solve problems. Maybe some of you are thinking about your research skills, your ability to draw together information from different sources and synthesize it into a plan of action. I'm sure there are many other possible answers that you could have thought of. My view is that if, like me, you're a senior individual contributor at a large organization, the single skill which contributes most to your effectiveness in your role is influence. I would wager that's also true for any of you that hold senior engineering management roles. Let's talk about influence.

I'm a senior architect responsible for the teams in the BBC's audio backend. Just to give a flavor of what those teams do, they deliver the backend functionality for the BBC's audio offering. On BBC Sounds, the BBC's flagship audio experience where they serve an audience of 4.8 million weekly active users. On third party platforms like Apple and Spotify, where the BBC's RSS platform is responsible for 85 million content downloads a month.

I'm sure some of you are thinking, why influence? There are many facets to a senior individual contributor role. Why do I want to talk to you about this one? I want to talk to you today about influence, because I've spent a lot of time in the last few years thinking about it. My career at the BBC has seen me move between different roles and different teams, from engineer to senior engineer, then principal engineer, and now architect. In those different roles, I've seen firsthand the power that good influence can have, and what can happen when influence is used in the wrong way. I've also found myself frustrated when I haven't been able to influence a decision in the way that I want to. Why couldn't I persuade that individual or group to adopt the approach I'm suggesting? What could I have done differently that might have led to a different outcome?

Another reason that I want to talk about influence is that it's about communication. Communication really fascinates me. Language is so powerful, so versatile, but also so full of nuance. I love exploring it and understanding how I can make better use of the potential power of my words. The English language leaves an awful lot of room for ambiguity, for accidental implication or for misunderstanding. Ultimately, while senior IC roles are very technical, they're also all about communication. The phrase individual contributor might imply that you sit in a corner on your own being awesome and smashing out contributions, but the reality in large organizations is that you spend far more of your time communicating than you do writing code or creating designs. Even the code that we do write and the designs and documents we create are forms of communication. Ultimately, we're all expressing and communicating ideas all the time in different ways.

Finally, I want to talk about influence because it feels particularly significant for architects. Now, not all organizations have architecture as a separate role from engineering. Some will use senior principal or other staff-plus roles to fulfill a lot of the same duties around technical strategy and technical leadership. At the BBC, architecture sits as a distinct discipline from engineering, which can lead to teams lacking understanding of what architecture's role is and being unsure as to how they should respond if their architect is telling them something they don't understand or is giving them direction that might not match the direction that their colleagues in engineering are giving them. The man in the picture here is the man none of us want to be and none of us want to work with. The architect in the ivory tower handing down their perfect designs, but devoid of context about how those designs will be implemented and become a practical reality.

They might have influence, but if they do, they're using it in the wrong way. The difference between the ivory tower architect, someone who is likely to be isolated, might be disliked and definitely won't be effective, and the friendly neighborhood architect who the team want to work with and who helps them solve problems is all about communication and all about influence.

What do we really mean when we talk about influence in the context of senior IC roles? Let's start with this dictionary definition. There are some useful aspects to this, in particular around our ability to have an effect on someone or something, and focusing on the character, development, or behavior of that personal thing. As senior individual contributors, we're often trying to influence behaviors of people or teams, when we want to influence process or ways of working, or we're trying to influence the character and development of the software being built by leading teams to make good technical decisions. Influence is so key to these roles. Without it, it's really hard to be effective in the space. There are likely to be many different targets that you might be trying to influence in different situations. The teams that you have technical responsibility for, the senior leadership in your area, and other disciplines you work with, like product, UX, and architecture or engineering.

Influence for these roles is not the same as managerial authority. Managers still need the ability to influence their staff beyond just saying, I'm your boss, please do as I ask. Nonetheless, there is a reasonable expectation that if your boss asks you to do something, you'll probably do it. Senior IC roles can't rely on that. They need to build reputation with the individuals and teams they're trying to influence. That generally revolves around building relationships. One analogy which I sometimes find useful to consider when we talk about influence is to think of it as a catalyst. We can build our influence by nurturing our relationships, proving ourselves useful to the teams and individuals we work with, being measured in our steer and our interventions. This influence gives us power when significant decisions need to be made and can be used to push technical decision-making forward at key inflection points.

I hope if you give me the benefit of your time today, you'll be able to take a few things away from this talk. Specifically, I intend to give you some tools or techniques you can use to influence the teams and stakeholders you interact with. I'm going to cover my experiences using these tools in different situations. I hope you'll see some parallels with your own teams and projects. You'll ultimately be able to leverage something from this talk to be more effective in your own role.

The project I'm going to focus on for this talk is a large-scale re-architecture within BBC Sounds, which was started around a year ago. This is part of wider org changes to move to the product operating model and start to embrace platform engineering. Why is this project important? Because the BBC needs to evolve its digital offering to stay relevant. The BBC's audio offering is a key part of the digital estate and we need to ensure that it's in a fit state to serve the audience. First, I want to cover the project context and the organizational changes at the heart of it. The previous team structure was organized around a product vertical for BBC Sounds. Within that vertical, a catalog team provided core metadata for available audio content. A business-led team consumed that metadata and defined the business logic which powers the BBC Sounds experience. That business logic was used to serve the audience-facing experience across clients on web, mobile, TV devices, and smart speakers.

With the move to platform engineering, this structure needed to change. Under the new structure, the catalog team would sit in platform and the previous business-led team would be split into two halves, one half providing platform APIs. The remaining part of that team would sit within the experiences area of the org, and the audience-facing client teams would also sit within experiences. What would that mean for the split of responsibilities for those new teams? The platform team would own core and personalized metadata with responsibility for creating APIs that describe the catalog of on-demand content, including podcasts, previously aired radio programs, and audiobooks, and live content, the BBC's stable of local and national radio stations. The experience team would own personalization and user experience concerns, building personalized responses based on user context, and owning the logic around experience-specific concerns, such as what content rails are presented in clients, and experience variants, such as the international mode which users are presented with when using the app on holiday.

Given that high-level context, I'm now going to drill into some of the complexities around this project and the challenges and opportunities they present when looking at them through the lens of influence. On the technical front, there were various complexities in the BBC Sounds backend landscape to contend with. The technical estate was complex, consisting of over 40 separate microservices with varying degrees of team knowledge and documentation. This is a very zoomed-out view of the estate, just to give you a little flavor of the number of connections and the number of dependencies between different microservices. Some of these key services lacked separation of concerns, mixing personalization, in particular details of user activity, with core API responses. This included the program metadata service, which I'll come back to a little bit more later on. Let's think about those system characteristics, complexity and choices about separation of concerns. We saw in the dictionary definition earlier that influence is about our ability to have an effect on the character of people or things.

Persuading teams to revisit design decisions requires influence. The original estate design prioritized performant responses rather than service decoupling. Additionally, inter-service communication was handled via an RPC implementation using Thrift, built using Finatra and Finagle, which are no longer actively maintained. There was also a desire among platform engineering leadership to move away from the tech stack currently used in the estate. Existing services were built using Scala and there was a strong desire to move towards this tech stack that was more commonly used at the BBC due to issues with recruitment, retention, and knowledge sharing. Through our influence lens, this second complexity is about behavior. If we're seeking to change the day-to-day behaviors of a team who are used to using a given set of tools and ask them to learn and use something different, understandably there could be some reluctance to make that change, and this is where our ability to influence becomes key.

The project also had social complexities. The team had previously operated using a monolithic team structure. There were three engineering teams consisting of 20-plus engineers across dev and test but they'd operated as one large team for over 5 years. There was also an inconsistency around buy-in levels within the team. Attempts to split the team had been attempted before and resisted, and not all members of the existing team were in favor of a split either from a technical point of view or an organizational point of view. Both factors ultimately pointed to a need to try and increase buy-in in order to help with morale and ensure progress on the project. Most social complexities are ultimately about our ability to influence behaviors, and from experience these situations can be really tricky. People problems are almost always harder than technical problems. Finally, there were complexities on the operational front that we needed to consider.

Most significantly this is a high traffic system powering a key audience-facing experience, so there was a need to ensure that the audience experience was not adversely impacted by any of the re-architecture work. On the out-of-hours support front, previously all services had been managed using a single on-call rota leaving a need to consider how to move to clear our ownership boundaries and separate on-call responsibilities across the platform and experience divide but without impacting our operational response. Looked at through our influence lens, again there's a desire to have an effect on system characteristics. We want the system to change but we don't want that to impact the audience, and there is a desire to have an effect on the team's behavior without degrading the operational outcomes.

Given that context, what was my approach? The first steps involved selling the vision to the team. The initial work was to sell the benefits of the change to the team and help them understand why we were doing this. The first key benefit was around increasing the speed of delivery. I'm firmly of the belief that smaller teams with more manageable technical estates can more easily reason about those technical estates and feel confident that they understand everything they're responsible for. This leads to engineers having less fear and greater confidence to evolve the software that they own. Additionally, this change will begin to unlock cross-functional audience experiences which weren't previously possible within the BBC digital estate, such as cross-experience recommendations. Many of you may be fans of "The Traitors," and may also be aware of the companion podcast, "The Traitors: Uncloaked." At present it's not possible to recommend the companion podcast to viewers of the show on iPlayer, and the move towards a platform engineering stance where generic capabilities are exposed to a variety of teams is a key part of breaking down those silos and enabling these richer audience experiences.

I also needed to set expectation with the teams that this change wasn't optional. There was a clear strategy being set by senior leadership and a need to align around that strategy. This kind of project presents key tensions for anyone in an IC role, and that's because those roles rely on building and maintaining strong positive relationships with the teams and individuals you interact with. Operational strategy can't be ignored but the way that you implement that strategy can have a huge impact on your relationships within an organization. This is where we come to the first couple of tools in the influence toolkit. In order to sell the vision, I land on two things. Spoken communication either in person or via video calls is a huge part of the way that we influence people. That spoken communication can be one-to-one or in groups sometimes aided by presenting from slides or talking about documents.

It's absolutely essential to communicate the vision and build rapport across all levels and disciplines, whether that's engineering, delivery, product, architecture, UX, whatever disciplines you might happen to have in your organization. When I'm speaking to people and trying to sell a vision, I try and make space to allow time for questions and challenges, and to engage honestly with the doubts and fears that individuals might have about what's being proposed. Spoken communication is valuable but it doesn't always scale. If you're trying to influence a group of 30 or even 100, that's an awful lot of one-to-one interactions. This is where context documentation comes in. I led on the creation of context documentation that could be used to disseminate the vision to the wider team, and I collaborated closely with key engineers to outline the problem, the challenges, the rationale, and the planned next steps.

Inevitably, during this vision setting period, there were some areas of pushback from some members of the team and I had to address those. One of the most significant areas of pushback was the view that we didn't have enough idea of future vision or future requirements to inform our approach for changing the technical estate. To address this, I liaised closely with colleagues in product and established that there were no concrete or hypothetical requirements that would be impeded by the proposed approach. Another really significant area of pushback was the view that doing this properly would take three years and anything else would be a bodge. Ultimately, my response to that was quite simple. We don't have the luxury of indulging in 3-year re-architecture projects which don't deliver audience-facing value. Tradeoffs would be required but this change represents an acceptable first step in the evolution of the estate.

When we're thinking about pushback, it can be useful to think about individuals and teams in the matrix of support and resistance. In the top right you've got active supporters. These people are thoroughly bought into whatever you're proposing and whatever you're trying to achieve. They're already cheerleading what you're doing so you shouldn't need to spend any time influencing them, and they should help in your ability to influence others because they're actively supporting your efforts. In the top left you've got passive supporters. They're not so vocal in their support either because they don't care enough or because they're not comfortable evangelizing to a wider team. You shouldn't need to spend that much time influencing here either but you're unlikely to get active help. In the bottom left you'll find passive resistors. They're opposed to your idea or your plan, but they're not doing anything to really try and prevent things from happening.

Passive resistance can have an impact on morale because it can lead to grumbling. It's worth identifying anyone in this camp and spending some time trying to influence them, but they're definitely not the key group. Down in the bottom right you've got the active resistors. They're opposed to the idea or the plan and they're trying to head in another direction. This can manifest in a few different ways. Active resistance can involve arguing or dissenting in group discussions or in discussions one-to-one, but it can also present in a less obvious way where people say nothing but quietly keep on doing something that doesn't align with the strategy. The active resistors are the group that you should spend most of your time trying to influence, and they will often represent a disproportionately small number of people or teams within your overall sphere of responsibility. If you can influence these individuals to move to passive support or even active support, your ability to drive change will be hugely improved.

Back to the re-architecture. With the team aligned around the vision, the next step was to break down the problem into manageable chunks and identify the key areas that the teams would need to agree approaches for. I collaborated with stakeholders and discipline leads to identify the areas where significant changes would be required and where agreement would need to be reached. That included ways of working, how the teams would interact as they split apart, and how we would approach the work for the re-architecture. How the teams would approach AWS account management given that up until that point all infrastructure resources had been deployed to a single set of accounts. Agreeing ownership of the services in the existing estate between the new teams. Agreeing an approach to common libraries and whether there would be a need to adopt an InnerSource model. Looking at a strategy for contract testing to validate the new boundary between platform and experience teams.

Lastly, thinking about how to split functionality in the services at the heart of the estate which needed to change to support the re-architecture. When it comes to achieving consensus, I'm a huge fan of the combined process of RFCs and ADRs, which the teams I was working with in this instance were already familiar with. RFCs, that's request for comment documents, are a powerful starting point for decision-making. I led the creation of an RFC for each significant problem area. The process around RFCs allows for collaboration with key players, and then once you have consensus in a tight group you can widen the group you're seeking input from. This process really empowers good analysis, letting you tease out ideas, gain input, come to consensus, and push decision-making forward. Once each of these RFCs had come to a conclusion, decisions were documented using ADRs. That stands for architecture decision record.

If anybody isn't familiar with the idea of ADRs I really encourage you to look up this blog post by Michael Nygard. It's an excellent rundown of the concept behind that particular kind of documentation. ADRs provide a perfect format to ensure that key decisions are documented tersely for future reference. Documentation is really powerful but it's not enough on its own. It's also necessary to have regular check-ins with your stakeholders. These can be used to identify any remaining points of contention, have any debates that are still necessary. They provide an opportunity to really push for progress, to ask the group to find the compromise, ask if things are really a problem, and agree an approach so that you can move forward and not get bogged down.

A big part of selling this vision was in helping the teams to understand the long-term strategy but also sending the message that this wasn't the end state, rather a useful stepping stone to allow further evolution of the estate as we evolve the audio offering in line with wider BBC digital plans. Viewing things through that lens, a number of tradeoffs and compromises were accepted. Initially, work on the platform side would create an API on a parity basis, so a newly owned API which provides the same functionality and a very similar API surface to the existing core service. This is probably not the API shape that we would choose if we were designing the API from scratch, and it will undoubtedly require further evolution. Attempting to redesign the API while also splitting the technical estate would have been too complicated and would have introduced unacceptable delays. A greater degree of coupling between platform and experience services than is ultimately desirable will persist for some time after the initial re-architecture work is complete.

I consider this an acceptable tradeoff to reach a point of separate autonomous teams that are then empowered to further change their technical estates and continue to evolve the system's architecture towards new goals and requirements. A transitionary approach would be required around operational support. Out-of-hours rotas and the handling of business-as-usual maintenance tasks would not be able to immediately match the desired team structures, and this would be necessary to ensure that operational stability wasn't impacted by the re-architecture work.

I can't cover every facet of a project this large, so I'm going to zoom in on some areas where I feel my influence was particularly useful, starting with some decisions around the tech stack used by the platform API team. The team had taken a decision to use Node.js, moving away from Scala. I identified this as an opportunity to leverage the existing approach used in sister teams, such as the catalog team, and I leaned on my experience in those teams where I'd previously laid the foundations of a monorepo approach using CDK for infrastructure and CI/CD. I shared lots of prior art with the new platform team, including code samples and documentation. I conducted targeted knowledge sharing sessions with the team lead and the principal engineer in that space to ensure that they understood the rationale and advantages inherent in the approaches that I was sharing with them.

I was also influential in guiding the team towards a managed service approach, an opportunity to move away from the maintenance burden associated with running services on EC2, which was heavily used in the previous estate. I suggested that the team should make more use of managed services, such as Lambda and ECS Fargate, and pushed the team to consider the tradeoffs and use the most managed solution wherever possible to keep overheads low, taking a serverless-first approach and only falling back to serverful options where compelling reasons existed. Back to the influence toolkit, these are the techniques that I lean on when I'm working on the ground with teams. Slack is such a valuable tool for collaboration, and it offers really unique opportunities to influence behavior and decision-making. Being present in team channels and observing day-to-day discussions provides valuable opportunities and allows you to spot technical problems or decision points where there might be an opportunity to share prior approaches or leverage existing organizational knowledge.

Slack is so rich. You can link to other Slack conversations, GitHub examples, documentation, blog posts, anything you like. While Slack is a powerful tool, it's really important that you follow up on those discussions. Speak to the key players and make yourself available to answer questions and dig into the detail. Ultimately, the aim here is to empower the team to use tried and tested patterns as a springboard to deliver faster, but also to upgrade or evolve those approaches where newer libraries or tools might be more powerful.

The second area I'd like to zoom in on is work around the core program metadata service, which I mentioned earlier on. Before the org change had been announced, work had been planned to remove Thrift from the BBC Sounds estate in order to address security vulnerabilities in the underlying Finatra and Finagle libraries used in the implementation. Due to the complexity of the service implementation, this was many sprints of work for a large number of engineers. That work would ultimately be thrown away in less than a year due to replacement functionality being created in the platform space. Once I'd identified this risk, I raised the issue with senior leadership. There was pushback from the team around the security considerations and the difficulties associated with changing the team's roadmap at short notice. Ultimately, I secured agreement for a change of approach. Once we were further into the re-architecture project, discussions around how to split the core program metadata service began, and the engineers began to think about how far to go with the re-architecture work.

Some of the engineers were keen to look at a larger reimagination of how personalization might work across the estate. I identified this as a source of risk in terms of project timelines. A more complex reimagination could quickly grow arms and legs, leading to elongated project timelines and blocking any work which could deliver audience value. I pushed strongly for the team to distill options with a focus on simplicity and speed of delivery rather than notions of elegance or wider scope. Not a hack, but a pragmatic path forward.

Some of the discussions around the core program metadata service were difficult, with significant differences of opinion among stakeholders. Perhaps the most important part of the influence toolkit is how we use our influence to have those difficult discussions. Having allies is absolutely essential, whether that's your boss, your peers, or other key stakeholders on the projects that you're working on. That's because the best ideas and the strongest visions will still fail to gain traction if you don't have support, because change is hard. Finally, when approaching tricky discussions, radical candor can be hugely powerful. We need to be willing to have difficult conversations, approach them head-on, and be frank in the way that we address problems. It's important to ensure that we do the right thing, not the easy thing. I'm lifting a quote here from Kim Scott's book entitled, "Radical Candor," caring personally while challenging directly. Scott was talking about management, but I think the same principle applies to influence. If we build a reputation as a caring and empathetic co-worker, we build our influence. When we have good relationships with the people we're trying to influence, then we gain the ability to challenge directly and move discussions forward.

I want to touch on how to measure success. I want to bookend the re-architecture story by covering our progress so far. We're not finished, but we're on track. Agreement has been reached on all the major decision points, and those decisions have all been documented in ADRs for future reference. The platform team have already made a lot of great progress towards creating a new API surface, and the building experiences to integrate with those new APIs is also underway. Now comes the trickier part, what could have gone better? At times, morale in the team has not felt as high as I might have liked. Change is hard, and there are many factors that affect how people feel, but ultimately this points to an area that I could have had more success. I'm not sure there's any such thing as perfect morale, but that doesn't mean we should ever stop trying to find it.

Some of my personal approaches weren't as successful as I'd hoped. Every individual is different, and it often takes time to establish the best way to interact with them. It can be hard to affect positive change when you don't have prior relationships to lean on, or if you're geographically at a distance from the person or team that you're trying to interact with. Sometimes my approach was wide of the mark, and I've tried to learn from those experiences. In terms of buy-in, I think my attempts at vision selling fell short with some members of the team. Now, 100% buy-in is probably unrealistic for a change of any significance, and I remain a big believer in the concept of disagree and commit. Nonetheless, there may have been ways that my vision selling could have been improved.

How do you measure success? How do you tell whether you're any good at influencing the individuals and teams around you? When you're looking to measure your influence around areas of technical complexity, you can track your success by the technical decisions the teams are making. What proportion of those decisions are roughly in line with your desired outcome? How much are those decisions deviating from what you might consider perfect? Reviewing these technical milestones frequently can help you get a feel for the success of your influence. Measuring influence on areas of social and operational complexity is potentially more difficult. You're looking to influence people's behaviors, but behavior can be hard to observe, and individuals won't always be honest about how they truly feel. Outcomes may be harder to track, but you can look for clues. Does morale feel higher? Are you having less difficult conversations? Are you able to classify any of the active resistors you've encountered as passive resistors or as supporters?

The best thing you can do is ask for feedback. Check in with your stakeholders and your teams. Ask them to give an honest assessment of how you're doing. If you feel brave, you can ask someone you often seem to disagree with to give you feedback. You might find something you can learn from and be able to incorporate into your practice, whether that's positive or negative.

The nature of feedback and the different ways we can receive it is something I want to touch on, because feedback comes in different forms, and these different signals can help us understand whether our influence is working in the way we want it to. When people think about feedback, they often mean direct feedback. Either you're actively asking someone to tell you how you're doing or to reflect on their interactions with you over the past six months, perhaps. Or someone has something they wish to address with you, and they provide direct feedback without request. Now, that kind of feedback is really useful, especially if you haven't had to ask for it. That means the person you're interacting with really wanted to tell you something, and that's something that you can always learn from, whether it's positive or negative. You can also get some really valuable insights from indirect feedback, and this is where relationships come in.

If you have friendly, positive relationships with the people around you, then the conversations you have can give you valuable indications of the success of your influence. To give an example, I bumped into one of the engineers in the platform API team a few months ago in the office, and I had a short conversation where I asked them how everything was going. They mentioned how positive they'd found the experience of moving into the new team structure and using the new tech stack, and how much more quickly the team were able to build things in this new world compared to their previous experience. These kinds of conversations could easily be dismissed as small talk, where nothing of value is likely to be learned, but in this case, I received an anecdotal indicator. The approach I'd proposed was working for the team. This kind of positive feedback loop, where we make helpful suggestions to teams, is how we build trust and ultimately grow our influence.

Let's recap the tools I've talked about in the influence toolkit. Spoken communication is so powerful. Find opportunities to talk to people, whether that's one-to-one, in groups, over a coffee, in workshops, whatever settings present themselves to you and feel right. Consider context documentation when you're trying to sell a vision to a big team, and use it to scale your influence beyond what can be achieved in one-to-one conversations. Leverage the power of the RFC and ADR process to build consensus and really drive decision-making. Make sure you review regularly with stakeholders around those decisions and keep key players in the loop. Spend time on the ground with your teams. Try and understand the challenges they face, and use tools like Slack to find opportunities to help and guide them. When you share thoughts with your teams in this way, make sure that you follow up. Make time to continue the discussions in the most appropriate way and drill into the detail. Build a network of allies so that your vision is nurtured and you have support when you need it for difficult conversations. Practice radical candor. Build your relationships and be prepared to challenge directly so that you can help your teams to make the right decisions.

Martell: You talked some about how we need to work to get our teams to buy into our vision. Sometimes you're in a place where the vision maybe isn't yours, and you need to get the team to buy into it. Maybe you're not 1,000% aligned. What does that look like? Other than disagree and commit, how do we do that?

Henry Wilson: That's really hard. Sometimes in senior leadership positions, we do get put in a position where the organizational strategy is moving in a certain direction, and it's not necessarily a direction we would have chosen. Ideally you would get some opportunity to feed into that technical direction. You would have the opportunity to talk to senior leadership and challenge, try and influence the direction that's moving in. I think if you aren't successful in that, if the organization is moving in a direction that you disagree with, you do have to disagree and commit. Either that or you have to find another job. That's a really hard position to be in. I think it asks a lot of people to positively sell a vision they don't truly believe in. I suppose you have to ask yourself how much you disagree with this. I think if you disagree with it too much, then maybe you do need to find another job.

Participant 1: What were the biggest challenges from the active resistors and how you tackled those?

Henry Wilson: I think the challenges in this case were, yes, I think there was a lot of pushback about whether this was something that we really wanted to do and whether it was being pursued for the right reasons. When you're dealing with technical teams that have been in place for a long time, regardless of what job title somebody might have or what seniority they technically hold, people who are long established in teams can have a lot of influence. I think that, yes, that presents challenges if key players are grumbling, and espousing a view that we shouldn't be doing this or that this is a waste of time or that it's doomed to failure in some way. There are no easy answers to those kinds of problems, unfortunately. You have to try and get people on side, try and explain the rationale for changes, explain why as an organization you're pursuing a given strategy, but yes, it can be difficult. Some people have very strong opinions and are very stuck in their ways.

Participant 2: How can you choose what hills to die on, if you know what I mean, and just like when you're butting heads with someone and you're like, do I let this go, do I drop it, or you're like, actually no, I really want to pursue this.

Henry Wilson: That's a really tricky judgment call. I think some of it has to be about how significant the change really is. I think you definitely have to try and identify as objectively as you can which areas are really significant, where there's some significant risk. Whether that's to do with timelines or to do with like ongoing maintenance, and you should try harder to persuade people, and where actually the direction they're heading in might not be the one that you would choose. It's more of a toss-up decision, at which point if you argue the toss over every one of those, then you're probably going to make yourself quite unpopular. I think the other thing to bear in mind is where there's an opportunity for learning. I think there's an element with these kind of IC roles where you can get into, trust me I'm a doctor mode.

Often, people will learn more from their own tried and tested experience of having gone down the wrong path and found out for themselves why it was the wrong path. I think there's a really interesting judgment call. Sometimes you can see that an approach is wrong, but it's still better to let the team learn that firsthand than to prescribe it or try and prohibit them from pursuing it. There's a really difficult judgment call there around, I suppose, effectively how much time is consumed in allowing an individual or a team to go down that path, and if it feels like a reasonable tradeoff of, ok, we'll lose a couple of weeks, but they'll learn something really valuable, then maybe you let them do it. If it feels like they're going to lose six months, then maybe you shouldn't.

Participant 3: I was just wondering if you've ever been in a situation where engaging somebody who you initially view as like an active resistor has led you to, I suppose, switch to their side or change your initial direction that you wanted to influence them in.

Henry Wilson: That isn't so relevant when you're talking about organizational strategy because you're not going to be terribly popular if you start off trying to sell a vision of organizational strategy and then start trying to undermine it. I think when it comes to slightly less totemic technical decisions, it's really important to try and approach those discussions with an open mind. Inevitably, I think all of us when we go into technical discussions, we're going to have some idea of what we think the best outcome to that discussion is, but we're not doing a great job if we're set in that view to the point where nothing that can happen in the discussion is going to influence it otherwise. I think we have to be open to the possibility that somebody could persuade us of a different point of view. Personally, I find that quite refreshing. If I've come in with an idea and then somebody succeeds in persuading me that a different approach would be better, then I've learned something that day and that's really valuable.

Yes, I think it's about trying to be as objective as possible when we consider these things, and trying to make sure that we're doing things on the merit of the technical approach, the actual objective reality as much as we can assess it of what the outcomes are going to be like, rather than notions of pet ideas or personal opinions about who might be voicing the idea. That makes it sound really easy. It's not. Like you walk into a discussion with some preconceived ideas and some biases, it's difficult sometimes to challenge your own assumptions, but yes, it's worth doing.

#9925. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.
